passages.title: Children's names announce a broken relationship
passages.summary: The LORD’s word comes to Hosea in the days of King Jeroboam of Israel. God tells him to marry an unfaithful woman, since the land is unfaithful. He marries Gomer, and she has three children. The first is named Jezreel, for blood shed there. The second is named “No Mercy.” The third is named “Not My People.” Yet Israel will one day be as many as the sand. Where they were called “not my people,” they will be called God’s children.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: The 2026 lesson connects unfaithfulness with a broken covenant relationship. How does the closing promise reverse the children’s names?

contextNote.title: Children's names announce a broken relationship
contextNote.text: Each child’s name carries a message people hear daily. The names grow harsher: a place of bloodshed, then no mercy. Verse 9 gives the third name and its reason. God says, “you are not my people.” That reverses his promise at the exodus (Exodus 6:7). Verse 10 begins with “Yet” and turns at once. It repeats the promise to Abraham of countless descendants (Genesis 22:17).

passages.title: Threatened loss turns toward renewed belonging
passages.summary: God speaks of Israel as a wife who has gone after other lovers. She thinks they gave her bread, wool, oil, and drink. She does not know that God gave her the grain and the wine. He will block her path and take back his gifts. Then he will lead her into the desert and speak kindly to her. She will call him “my husband.” He will betroth her to himself forever. He will say to “Not My People,” “You are my people.”
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: The lesson studies renewed belonging through God’s love and mercy. What words define the renewed relationship after the threats?

contextNote.title: Threatened loss turns toward renewed belonging
contextNote.text: The chapter says “therefore” three times (verses 6, 9, 14). The first two announce loss. The third surprises: God will court her again in the desert. Verses 19–20 list what he brings to the betrothal. He gives righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion, and faithfulness. These are the qualities the marriage lacked. Verse 23 then reverses the children’s names from chapter 1.

passages.title: A household waiting period explains public loss
passages.summary: The LORD tells Hosea to love a woman again, though she is unfaithful. This is how the LORD loves Israel, who turn to other gods. Hosea buys her for silver and barley. He tells her to stay with him many days and belong to no other man. He will wait for her in the same way. Israel too will live many days without king or sacrifice. Afterward they will return and seek the LORD and David their king.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: The lesson invites readers to consider God’s continued invitation to return. What details remain unknown about the unnamed woman?

contextNote.title: A household waiting period explains public loss
contextNote.text: This chapter is five verses long. Hosea pays partly in silver and partly in grain (verse 2). He then sets a time of waiting with no intimacy (verse 3). Verse 4 applies that to the nation. Israel will lose king, sacrifice, sacred stone, and idols alike. Both its proper supports and its false ones are removed. Verse 5 says the waiting ends in return, so it is a pause.

passages.title: Rejected knowledge reaches daily life and leadership
passages.summary: The LORD brings a charge against the people of the land. There is no truth, kindness, or knowledge of God. There is cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery. The land mourns, and even the animals waste away. God’s dispute is with the priests. His people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. The priests feed on the people’s sin. God will not punish the daughters, since the men themselves go to prostitutes.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: Why does the speech refuse to blame daughters alone?

contextNote.title: Rejected knowledge reaches daily life and leadership
contextNote.text: Verse 6 says the people perish for lack of knowledge. The lack is no accident. The priests have “rejected” knowledge and “forgotten” God’s law. Teaching was their work (Malachi 2:7). Verse 8 says they profit from the people’s sins. Verse 14 refuses to blame the women alone. The men lead in the wrong, so the daughters are not singled out.

passages.title: Foreign help cannot heal the wound
passages.summary: God calls the priests, the people, and the royal house to listen. They have been a trap for others. Their deeds will not let them return to God. They will seek the LORD with flocks and not find him. Judah’s leaders are like men who move boundary stones. God is like a moth to Ephraim and like rot to Judah. Ephraim saw its sickness and sent to the king of Assyria. He cannot heal them, and God will wait until they seek him.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: Why can Assyria not cure the wound described here?

contextNote.title: Foreign help cannot heal the wound
contextNote.text: Verse 12 says God himself is the moth and the rot. The nation’s sickness comes from him. In verse 13 Ephraim notices the illness and chooses a doctor. It goes to Assyria and sends to King Jareb. Second Kings 15:19 and 17:3 record such payments. Assyria cannot cure what God is causing. Verse 15 says God will withdraw until they admit their guilt.

passages.title: Quick promises meet a charge of disappearing love
passages.summary: The people say, “Let’s return to the LORD.” He has torn them, and he will heal them. He will revive them and come like the spring rain. God answers by asking what he can do with them. Their love is like a morning cloud and like dew that soon vanishes. He desires mercy and not sacrifice. He wants knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. Instead they have broken the covenant, and priests murder on the road.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: The lesson connects mercy with sincere devotion beyond outward religious acts. How do charges of violence challenge the opening promises?

contextNote.title: Quick promises meet a charge of disappearing love
contextNote.text: The words of verses 1–3 sound like true repentance. God’s reply in verse 4 is weary. The people expect him to be as sure as rain. Their own love lasts as long as mist. Verse 6 names what he wants: steady loving kindness, not offerings. Jesus quotes this verse twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). Verses 8–9 show what the people are still doing.

passages.title: Hidden heat and foolish flight explain failed rule
passages.summary: God would heal Israel, but its guilt keeps coming to light. Thieves break in, and bands raid outside. The people do not consider that God remembers. Plotters are like an oven that smolders all night and blazes at dawn. All their kings have fallen, and none calls on God. Ephraim is like a cake baked on one side. Ephraim is like a silly dove, calling to Egypt and flying to Assyria. God will spread his net over them.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: What dangers do the oven and dove reveal?

contextNote.title: Hidden heat and foolish flight explain failed rule
contextNote.text: Two pictures explain the kingdom’s failure. Verses 4–7 show an oven: plots heat up overnight and burn by morning. Second Kings 15 records four kings murdered in a few years. Verse 11 shows a dove that flutters between two empires. It has no fixed direction. Verse 9 adds that foreigners drain Ephraim’s strength unnoticed. Inside there is heat, and outside there is aimless flight.

passages.title: Made objects and chosen rulers cannot secure life
passages.summary: A trumpet warns that an enemy is coming like an eagle. Israel cries that it knows God, yet it has rejected what is good. The people set up kings without asking God. They made idols of silver and gold. God rejects the calf of Samaria. A workman made it, and it is not God. They sow the wind and will reap the whirlwind. Israel has forgotten its Maker and built palaces.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: Why does naming the craftsman matter for the calf?

contextNote.title: Made objects and chosen rulers cannot secure life
contextNote.text: Verse 6 makes its case in a few words. A workman made the calf, so it is not God. The verse adds that it came “from Israel.” The idol is homemade. First Kings 12:28 tells how the calves were set up. Verse 4 says the same about the kings: made by the people, not by God. What people make for themselves cannot save its makers.

passages.title: Celebration gives way to lost land and children
passages.summary: Hosea tells Israel not to rejoice at the harvest. The people have been unfaithful on every threshing floor. They will not stay in the LORD’s land. They will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria. They will have no offerings to bring on feast days. The days of reckoning have come. The people call the prophet a fool and the inspired man mad. Their children will be lost, and they will wander among the nations.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: How does lost land affect worship as well as food?

contextNote.title: Celebration gives way to lost land and children
contextNote.text: The setting is a harvest festival (verse 1). Hosea says the celebration will end. Verses 3–5 link land and worship. In a foreign land there will be no wine offering and no feast. Verse 7 then shows how the nation treats its prophets. It calls them fools and madmen. The verse gives the cause: the people’s great guilt and hostility.

passages.title: Prosperity has cultivated the wrong harvest
passages.summary: Israel is a spreading vine that bears much fruit. The more it prospered, the more altars it built. Its heart is divided. The calf of Bethel will be carried to Assyria as a gift. Samaria’s king will vanish like a twig on water. God tells them to sow righteousness and reap kindness. They must break up their unplowed ground and seek the LORD. Instead they have plowed wickedness and trusted in their soldiers.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: What would a different harvest require from the people?

contextNote.title: Prosperity has cultivated the wrong harvest
contextNote.text: This chapter speaks in farming terms throughout. Verse 1 says prosperity fed the building of altars. Verse 12 describes a different crop. The people must sow what is right and break new ground. Unplowed ground takes hard work to open. Then they must wait for God to send rain. Verse 13 says what they planted in its place: wickedness and lies.

passages.title: Remembered care interrupts the threat of destruction
passages.summary: God says he loved Israel as a child and called his son out of Egypt. The more he called, the more they went away. He taught Ephraim to walk and carried them in his arms. He bent down and fed them. Now they refuse to return, and the sword will come. Then God asks how he can give them up. His heart turns over, and his compassion grows warm. He will roar like a lion, and his children will come trembling home.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: How does the lion’s role change at the end?

contextNote.title: Remembered care interrupts the threat of destruction
contextNote.text: Verses 1–4 are a parent’s memories of a small child. Verse 8 asks four questions in a row. God seems to argue with himself. Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). Verse 9 gives his reason for holding back. He is God and not a man. In verse 10 the lion’s roar calls the children home.

passages.title: Remembered Jacob challenges wealth without justice
passages.summary: Ephraim chases the wind and makes treaties with Assyria and Egypt. The LORD has a charge against Judah and Jacob. In the womb Jacob grasped his brother’s heel. As a man he struggled with God, wept, and asked for favor. So the people must turn to their God. They must keep kindness and justice and wait for him. A merchant with false scales loves to cheat. Ephraim says its wealth proves it has done no wrong.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: How do memories of Jacob challenge dishonest wealth?

contextNote.title: Remembered Jacob challenges wealth without justice
contextNote.text: Hosea holds up Jacob as a mirror for his descendants. Jacob began as a grasper (verse 3). He also wrestled, wept, and sought God’s favor (verse 4). Verse 6 says “Therefore” and applies it. The people must turn as he did. It names three duties: kindness, justice, and waiting. Verses 7–8 show the opposite: false scales and pride in wealth.

passages.title: Forgotten care gives way to destructive power
passages.summary: Ephraim once spoke and others trembled, but he died through Baal. Now the people make silver idols and kiss calves. They will vanish like morning mist. Yet the LORD has been their God since Egypt. He cared for them in the desert. When they were fed, they grew proud and forgot him. So he will meet them like a lion and a bear. Their kings cannot save them, and Samaria will bear its guilt.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: Why does remembered care make forgetfulness more serious?

contextNote.title: Forgotten care gives way to destructive power
contextNote.text: Verse 4 states God’s claim: no savior exists besides him. Verse 5 recalls his care in a dry land. Verse 6 traces what went wrong in four steps. They were fed, they were satisfied, they grew proud, and they forgot. Deuteronomy 8:11–14 warned of that very sequence. Forgetting after such care is worse than never knowing. Verses 7–8 show the shepherd become a wild beast.

passages.title: Returning words replace false sources of help
passages.summary: Hosea calls Israel to return to the LORD. He tells them to bring words with them. They should ask God to forgive and accept their praise. They should say that Assyria cannot save them. They will not trust horses or call their handmade things gods. God says he will heal them and love them freely. He will be like dew to Israel. Israel will blossom like a lily and spread like an olive tree.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: The lesson studies freely given love and the blessings of repentance. How do the plant pictures reverse earlier losses?

contextNote.title: Returning words replace false sources of help
contextNote.text: Verses 2–3 give the people a prayer to say. It gives up three false helps named through the book. They are Assyria, war horses, and gods made by hand. Verse 4 gives God’s answer: he will love them “freely.” Their words do not buy it. In 6:4 dew stood for Israel’s vanishing love. In verse 5 God himself is the dew that makes them grow.

events.detail: Verse 12 says God himself is the moth and the rot. The nation’s sickness comes from him. In verse 13 Ephraim notices the illness and chooses a doctor. It goes to Assyria and sends to King Jareb. Second Kings 15:19 and 17:3 record such payments. Assyria cannot cure what God is causing. Verse 15 says God will withdraw until they admit their guilt.
events.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: Why can Assyria not cure the wound described here?

events.title: Quick promises meet a charge of disappearing love
events.summary: The people say, “Let’s return to the LORD.” He has torn them, and he will heal them. He will revive them and come like the spring rain. God answers by asking what he can do with them. Their love is like a morning cloud and like dew that soon vanishes. He desires mercy and not sacrifice. He wants knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. Instead they have broken the covenant, and priests murder on the road.
events.detail: The words of verses 1–3 sound like true repentance. God’s reply in verse 4 is weary. The people expect him to be as sure as rain. Their own love lasts as long as mist. Verse 6 names what he wants: steady loving kindness, not offerings. Jesus quotes this verse twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). Verses 8–9 show what the people are still doing.
events.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: The lesson connects mercy with sincere devotion beyond outward religious acts. How do charges of violence challenge the opening promises?

events.title: Hidden heat and foolish flight explain failed rule
events.summary: God would heal Israel, but its guilt keeps coming to light. Thieves break in, and bands raid outside. The people do not consider that God remembers. Plotters are like an oven that smolders all night and blazes at dawn. All their kings have fallen, and none calls on God. Ephraim is like a cake baked on one side. Ephraim is like a silly dove, calling to Egypt and flying to Assyria. God will spread his net over them.
events.detail: Two pictures explain the kingdom’s failure. Verses 4–7 show an oven: plots heat up overnight and burn by morning. Second Kings 15 records four kings murdered in a few years. Verse 11 shows a dove that flutters between two empires. It has no fixed direction. Verse 9 adds that foreigners drain Ephraim’s strength unnoticed. Inside there is heat, and outside there is aimless flight.
events.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: What dangers do the oven and dove reveal?

events.title: Made objects and chosen rulers cannot secure life
events.summary: A trumpet warns that an enemy is coming like an eagle. Israel cries that it knows God, yet it has rejected what is good. The people set up kings without asking God. They made idols of silver and gold. God rejects the calf of Samaria. A workman made it, and it is not God. They sow the wind and will reap the whirlwind. Israel has forgotten its Maker and built palaces.
events.detail: Verse 6 makes its case in a few words. A workman made the calf, so it is not God. The verse adds that it came “from Israel.” The idol is homemade. First Kings 12:28 tells how the calves were set up. Verse 4 says the same about the kings: made by the people, not by God. What people make for themselves cannot save its makers.
events.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: Why does naming the craftsman matter for the calf?

events.title: Celebration gives way to lost land and children
events.summary: Hosea tells Israel not to rejoice at the harvest. The people have been unfaithful on every threshing floor. They will not stay in the LORD’s land. They will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria. They will have no offerings to bring on feast days. The days of reckoning have come. The people call the prophet a fool and the inspired man mad. Their children will be lost, and they will wander among the nations.
events.detail: The setting is a harvest festival (verse 1). Hosea says the celebration will end. Verses 3–5 link land and worship. In a foreign land there will be no wine offering and no feast. Verse 7 then shows how the nation treats its prophets. It calls them fools and madmen. The verse gives the cause: the people’s great guilt and hostility.
events.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: How does lost land affect worship as well as food?

events.title: Prosperity has cultivated the wrong harvest
events.summary: Israel is a spreading vine that bears much fruit. The more it prospered, the more altars it built. Its heart is divided. The calf of Bethel will be carried to Assyria as a gift. Samaria’s king will vanish like a twig on water. God tells them to sow righteousness and reap kindness. They must break up their unplowed ground and seek the LORD. Instead they have plowed wickedness and trusted in their soldiers.
events.detail: This chapter speaks in farming terms throughout. Verse 1 says prosperity fed the building of altars. Verse 12 describes a different crop. The people must sow what is right and break new ground. Unplowed ground takes hard work to open. Then they must wait for God to send rain. Verse 13 says what they planted in its place: wickedness and lies.
events.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: What would a different harvest require from the people?

events.title: Remembered care interrupts the threat of destruction
events.summary: God says he loved Israel as a child and called his son out of Egypt. The more he called, the more they went away. He taught Ephraim to walk and carried them in his arms. He bent down and fed them. Now they refuse to return, and the sword will come. Then God asks how he can give them up. His heart turns over, and his compassion grows warm. He will roar like a lion, and his children will come trembling home.
events.detail: Verses 1–4 are a parent’s memories of a small child. Verse 8 asks four questions in a row. God seems to argue with himself. Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). Verse 9 gives his reason for holding back. He is God and not a man. In verse 10 the lion’s roar calls the children home.
events.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: How does the lion’s role change at the end?

events.title: Remembered Jacob challenges wealth without justice
events.summary: Ephraim chases the wind and makes treaties with Assyria and Egypt. The LORD has a charge against Judah and Jacob. In the womb Jacob grasped his brother’s heel. As a man he struggled with God, wept, and asked for favor. So the people must turn to their God. They must keep kindness and justice and wait for him. A merchant with false scales loves to cheat. Ephraim says its wealth proves it has done no wrong.
events.detail: Hosea holds up Jacob as a mirror for his descendants. Jacob began as a grasper (verse 3). He also wrestled, wept, and sought God’s favor (verse 4). Verse 6 says “Therefore” and applies it. The people must turn as he did. It names three duties: kindness, justice, and waiting. Verses 7–8 show the opposite: false scales and pride in wealth.
events.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: How do memories of Jacob challenge dishonest wealth?

events.title: Forgotten care gives way to destructive power
events.summary: Ephraim once spoke and others trembled, but he died through Baal. Now the people make silver idols and kiss calves. They will vanish like morning mist. Yet the LORD has been their God since Egypt. He cared for them in the desert. When they were fed, they grew proud and forgot him. So he will meet them like a lion and a bear. Their kings cannot save them, and Samaria will bear its guilt.
events.detail: Verse 4 states God’s claim: no savior exists besides him. Verse 5 recalls his care in a dry land. Verse 6 traces what went wrong in four steps. They were fed, they were satisfied, they grew proud, and they forgot. Deuteronomy 8:11–14 warned of that very sequence. Forgetting after such care is worse than never knowing. Verses 7–8 show the shepherd become a wild beast.
events.uncertainty: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.

lds.text: Why does remembered care make forgetfulness more serious?

events.title: Returning words replace false sources of help
events.summary: Hosea calls Israel to return to the LORD. He tells them to bring words with them. They should ask God to forgive and accept their praise. They should say that Assyria cannot save them. They will not trust horses or call their handmade things gods. God says he will heal them and love them freely. He will be like dew to Israel. Israel will blossom like a lily and spread like an olive tree.
events.detail: Verses 2–3 give the people a prayer to say. It gives up three false helps named through the book. They are Assyria, war horses, and gods made by hand. Verse 4 gives God’s answer: he will love them “freely.” Their words do not buy it. In 6:4 dew stood for Israel’s vanishing love. In verse 5 God himself is the dew that makes them grow.
events.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

lds.text: The lesson studies freely given love and the blessings of repentance. How do the plant pictures reverse earlier losses?

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Kingdom of Israel · approximate
regions.summary: Ten tribes followed Jeroboam and formed a northern kingdom. Samaria became its capital under Omri.
regions.detail: Kings and Chronicles follow its kings beside Judah’s. Assyria takes Samaria and deports its people in 2 Kings 17.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Its borders with Aram, Moab, and Judah moved often.

regions.name: Kingdom of Judah · approximate
regions.summary: Judah was the southern kingdom. David’s family ruled it from Jerusalem for about four centuries.
regions.detail: Judah keeps David’s line when the north breaks away. Its kings fight Israel, pay it, and join it by turns.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It is not a border for one year.

regions.name: Aram of Damascus · approximate
regions.summary: Aram was a kingdom centered on Damascus. Assyria ended it in 732 BCE.
regions.detail: Ben Hadad and Hazael fight Israel for Gilead. Naaman, healed in 2 Kings 5, commands Aram’s army.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Aram and Israel traded control of Gilead and Bashan.

regions.name: Phoenician cities · approximate
regions.summary: Tyre, Sidon, and other coast cities each had their own king. They lived by ships and trade.
regions.detail: Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians (1 Kings 16:31). Elijah stays with a widow at Zarephath near Sidon.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins separate cities along one coast. They were never one kingdom.

regions.name: Philistine cities · approximate
regions.summary: Five Philistine cities held the southern coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath.
regions.detail: Philistine towns sit on Judah’s western border. Israel besieges Gibbethon, a Philistine town, twice in 1 Kings 15–16.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Each city had its own ruler.

regions.name: Ammon · approximate
regions.summary: Ammon was a kingdom east of the Jordan. Its chief city was Rabbah, now Amman.
regions.detail: Ammon joins Moab against Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 20. Amos 1 accuses Ammon of cruelty in Gilead.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Rabbah.

regions.name: Moab · approximate
regions.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
regions.detail: Mesha king of Moab rebels after Ahab dies (2 Kings 3). A stone that Mesha set up tells his side.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

regions.name: Edom · approximate
regions.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
regions.detail: Edom revolts against Judah in the days of Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20–22). Amos 1 accuses Edom of chasing his brother with the sword.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

regions.name: Egypt · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt’s kings ruled the Nile valley and delta.
regions.detail: Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple treasures from Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25–26). Hosea warns Israel against calling on Egypt.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power changed across these centuries.

regions.name: Assyria · home region
regions.summary: Assyria’s home lay on the upper Tigris around Assur, Kalhu, and Nineveh. From 745 BCE its kings pushed hard to the west.
regions.detail: Menahem of Israel and Ahaz of Judah pay Assyria’s kings. Assyria takes Damascus, then Samaria, in 2 Kings 16–17.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows only the home region. Assyria’s reach to the west grew and shrank.

guides.title: Hosea: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Threatened loss turns toward renewed belonging
steps.text: The chapter says “therefore” three times (verses 6, 9, 14). The first two announce loss. The third surprises: God will court her again in the desert. Verses 19–20 list what he brings to the betrothal. He gives righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion, and faithfulness. These are the qualities the marriage lacked. Verse 23 then reverses the children’s names from chapter 1.

steps.title: Quick promises meet a charge of disappearing love
steps.text: The words of verses 1–3 sound like true repentance. God’s reply in verse 4 is weary. The people expect him to be as sure as rain. Their own love lasts as long as mist. Verse 6 names what he wants: steady loving kindness, not offerings. Jesus quotes this verse twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). Verses 8–9 show what the people are still doing.

steps.title: Remembered care interrupts the threat of destruction
steps.text: Verses 1–4 are a parent’s memories of a small child. Verse 8 asks four questions in a row. God seems to argue with himself. Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). Verse 9 gives his reason for holding back. He is God and not a man. In verse 10 the lion’s roar calls the children home.

chapterMaps.note: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.
chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD’s word comes to Hosea in the days of King Jeroboam of Israel. God tells him to marry an unfaithful woman, since the land is unfaithful. He marries Gomer, and she has three children. The first is named Jezreel, for blood shed there. The second is named “No Mercy.” The third is named “Not My People.” Yet Israel will one day be as many as the sand. Where they were called “not my people,” they will be called God’s children.
chapterMaps.limits: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show named places from the speeches. They do not show a route.
chapterMaps.narrative: God speaks of Israel as a wife who has gone after other lovers. She thinks they gave her bread, wool, oil, and drink. She does not know that God gave her the grain and the wine. He will block her path and take back his gifts. Then he will lead her into the desert and speak kindly to her. She will call him “my husband.” He will betroth her to himself forever. He will say to “Not My People,” “You are my people.”

chapterMaps.note: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.
chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Hosea to love a woman again, though she is unfaithful. This is how the LORD loves Israel, who turn to other gods. Hosea buys her for silver and barley. He tells her to stay with him many days and belong to no other man. He will wait for her in the same way. Israel too will live many days without king or sacrifice. Afterward they will return and seek the LORD and David their king.

chapterMaps.note: This chapter has no mapped places. Unnamed or uncertain settings stay off the map.
chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD brings a charge against the people of the land. There is no truth, kindness, or knowledge of God. There is cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery. The land mourns, and even the animals waste away. God’s dispute is with the priests. His people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. The priests feed on the people’s sin. God will not punish the daughters, since the men themselves go to prostitutes.

chapterMaps.narrative: God calls the priests, the people, and the royal house to listen. They have been a trap for others. Their deeds will not let them return to God. They will seek the LORD with flocks and not find him. Judah’s leaders are like men who move boundary stones. God is like a moth to Ephraim and like rot to Judah. Ephraim saw its sickness and sent to the king of Assyria. He cannot heal them, and God will wait until they seek him.

chapterMaps.narrative: The people say, “Let’s return to the LORD.” He has torn them, and he will heal them. He will revive them and come like the spring rain. God answers by asking what he can do with them. Their love is like a morning cloud and like dew that soon vanishes. He desires mercy and not sacrifice. He wants knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. Instead they have broken the covenant, and priests murder on the road.

chapterMaps.narrative: God would heal Israel, but its guilt keeps coming to light. Thieves break in, and bands raid outside. The people do not consider that God remembers. Plotters are like an oven that smolders all night and blazes at dawn. All their kings have fallen, and none calls on God. Ephraim is like a cake baked on one side. Ephraim is like a silly dove, calling to Egypt and flying to Assyria. God will spread his net over them.

chapterMaps.narrative: A trumpet warns that an enemy is coming like an eagle. Israel cries that it knows God, yet it has rejected what is good. The people set up kings without asking God. They made idols of silver and gold. God rejects the calf of Samaria. A workman made it, and it is not God. They sow the wind and will reap the whirlwind. Israel has forgotten its Maker and built palaces.

chapterMaps.narrative: Hosea tells Israel not to rejoice at the harvest. The people have been unfaithful on every threshing floor. They will not stay in the LORD’s land. They will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria. They will have no offerings to bring on feast days. The days of reckoning have come. The people call the prophet a fool and the inspired man mad. Their children will be lost, and they will wander among the nations.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel is a spreading vine that bears much fruit. The more it prospered, the more altars it built. Its heart is divided. The calf of Bethel will be carried to Assyria as a gift. Samaria’s king will vanish like a twig on water. God tells them to sow righteousness and reap kindness. They must break up their unplowed ground and seek the LORD. Instead they have plowed wickedness and trusted in their soldiers.

chapterMaps.narrative: God says he loved Israel as a child and called his son out of Egypt. The more he called, the more they went away. He taught Ephraim to walk and carried them in his arms. He bent down and fed them. Now they refuse to return, and the sword will come. Then God asks how he can give them up. His heart turns over, and his compassion grows warm. He will roar like a lion, and his children will come trembling home.

chapterMaps.narrative: Ephraim chases the wind and makes treaties with Assyria and Egypt. The LORD has a charge against Judah and Jacob. In the womb Jacob grasped his brother’s heel. As a man he struggled with God, wept, and asked for favor. So the people must turn to their God. They must keep kindness and justice and wait for him. A merchant with false scales loves to cheat. Ephraim says its wealth proves it has done no wrong.

chapterMaps.narrative: Ephraim once spoke and others trembled, but he died through Baal. Now the people make silver idols and kiss calves. They will vanish like morning mist. Yet the LORD has been their God since Egypt. He cared for them in the desert. When they were fed, they grew proud and forgot him. So he will meet them like a lion and a bear. Their kings cannot save them, and Samaria will bear its guilt.

chapterMaps.narrative: Hosea calls Israel to return to the LORD. He tells them to bring words with them. They should ask God to forgive and accept their praise. They should say that Assyria cannot save them. They will not trust horses or call their handmade things gods. God says he will heal them and love them freely. He will be like dew to Israel. Israel will blossom like a lily and spread like an olive tree.
